statement:
Implement an in-memory cloud storage system. The system only records each file's name and size, not its contents.

This problem is the same kind as Online Assessment: Cloud File Storage on this site, but what circulates here is a different set of operations: the interface is string commands, files can be deleted, you can get the n largest files under a prefix, and restoring a backup "restores as many as it can". The rules of the two pages differ; don't mix them up.

Every operation goes through one function:

def solution(queries: list[list[str]]) -> list[str]:
    """Run the queries in order on one storage that starts empty.
    Returns one string per query."""

Each command is a list of strings: the first element is the operation name, the rest are its arguments. All arguments are strings, and numbers are written in decimal (for example "10"). Each command returns a string: success or failure is "true" / "false", numbers are converted to decimal strings, and "no result" is the empty string "". What each operation returns exactly is described one by one below.

The problem has four levels, unlocked in order. Each level adds operations to the same system; the operations of earlier levels keep working, and their tests keep running too.

Conventions that apply to all four levels:

  • File names, user ids, and prefixes are non-empty strings without whitespace, and are case-sensitive. The file names in the examples look like paths (/dir/file.txt), but the system has no directories; a name is just an ordinary string.
  • At any moment, a name corresponds to at most one file, no matter who owns it.
  • size, capacity, and n are positive integers no greater than 109. A single call has at most 104 commands.
  • The input is guaranteed to be valid: the operation name is always one of those listed below, the number of arguments is right, and wherever a number is expected there is a number.
  • A failed command does not change any state.
  • Each level's example starts from an empty system.

Level 1 — Add, get, delete

  • ADD_FILE <name> <size>: add a file. Fails if a file with the same name already exists. Returns "true" on success and "false" on failure.
  • GET_FILE_SIZE <name>: return the file's size; returns "" if the file does not exist.
  • DELETE_FILE <name>: delete the file and return the size of the deleted file; returns "" if the file does not exist. After a deletion, the name can be used again.
["ADD_FILE", "/dir1/dir2/file.txt", "10"]    -> "true"
["ADD_FILE", "/dir1/dir2/file.txt", "5"]     -> "false"   # a file with this name exists; the size is still 10
["GET_FILE_SIZE", "/dir1/dir2/file.txt"]     -> "10"
["DELETE_FILE", "/not-existing.file"]        -> ""
["DELETE_FILE", "/dir1/dir2/file.txt"]       -> "10"
["GET_FILE_SIZE", "/not-existing.file"]      -> ""

Level 2 — The n largest files under a prefix

  • GET_N_LARGEST <prefix> <n>: among the files whose names start with prefix, take the n largest and return "<name1>(<size1>), <name2>(<size2>), ...".

Rules:

  • "Starts with prefix" is a plain string prefix (str.startswith), unrelated to directory levels: the prefix /dir/file matches /dir/file2 and /dir/file1.txt.
  • Sort by size, largest first; for equal sizes, sort by name in ascending lexicographic order (ordinary string comparison).
  • Items are separated by one comma and one space, ", ".
  • If fewer than n files match, return all of them. If none match, return "".
["ADD_FILE", "/dir/file1.txt", "5"]          -> "true"
["ADD_FILE", "/dir/file2", "20"]             -> "true"
["ADD_FILE", "/dir/deeper/file3.mov", "9"]   -> "true"
["GET_N_LARGEST", "/dir", "2"]               -> "/dir/file2(20), /dir/deeper/file3.mov(9)"
["GET_N_LARGEST", "/dir/file", "3"]          -> "/dir/file2(20), /dir/file1.txt(5)"     # only two match
["GET_N_LARGEST", "/another_dir", "2"]       -> ""
["ADD_FILE", "/big_file.mp4", "20"]          -> "true"
["GET_N_LARGEST", "/", "2"]                  -> "/big_file.mp4(20), /dir/file2(20)"     # sizes tie, so sort by name

Level 3 — Users and capacity

All users share one file system (names are still globally unique), but each user has a capacity limit: the total size of the files the user owns may not exceed it. A user's remaining capacity = capacity limit − total size of the files it currently owns.

  • ADD_USER <userId> <capacity>: create a user. Fails if the user already exists. Returns "true" on success and "false" on failure.
  • ADD_FILE_BY <userId> <name> <size>: add a file like ADD_FILE, but the file is owned by userId. Fails in any of these cases: the user does not exist; a file with the same name already exists (no matter who owns it); size is larger than the user's remaining capacity. On success returns the user's remaining capacity after the addition; on failure returns "". Using up the capacity exactly is allowed, and then it returns "0".
  • MERGE_USER <userId1> <userId2>: merge userId2 into userId1. All of userId2's files become owned by userId1; userId2's capacity limit is added to userId1's capacity limit (so the two remaining capacities also add up); then userId2 is deleted. Returns userId1's remaining capacity after the merge. If either user does not exist, or the two arguments are equal, it fails and returns "". The deleted user id can later be created again with ADD_USER, giving a brand-new, empty user.

This level also changes the meaning of the operations from the first two levels:

  • Level 1's ADD_FILE now counts as performed by the special user "admin". "admin" exists from the start and has unlimited capacity. The input guarantees that "admin" never appears as the userId of any operation that takes a userId argument (including the two Level 4 operations).
  • DELETE_FILE can delete any file, no matter who owns it. Deleting a user's file increases that user's remaining capacity accordingly.
  • GET_FILE_SIZE and GET_N_LARGEST still see all files, no matter who owns them.
["ADD_USER", "user1", "200"]                       -> "true"
["ADD_USER", "user1", "100"]                       -> "false"   # already exists; capacity is still 200
["ADD_FILE_BY", "user1", "/dir/file.med", "50"]    -> "150"
["ADD_FILE_BY", "user1", "/big.blob", "140"]       -> "10"
["ADD_FILE_BY", "user1", "/file-small", "20"]      -> ""        # only 10 left
["ADD_FILE", "/dir/admin_file", "300"]             -> "true"    # admin, unlimited capacity
["ADD_USER", "user2", "110"]                       -> "true"
["ADD_FILE_BY", "user2", "/dir/file.med", "45"]    -> ""        # a file with this name exists (owned by user1)
["ADD_FILE_BY", "user2", "/new_file", "50"]        -> "60"
["MERGE_USER", "user1", "user2"]                   -> "70"      # limit 200 + 110 = 310, used 190 + 50 = 240

Level 4 — Backup and restore

  • BACKUP_USER <userId>: record the names and sizes of all files userId currently owns. The backup is stored elsewhere, and no later operation on files changes it. Only the latest backup is kept per user; a new one replaces the old one. Returns the number of files in the backup (can be "0"); returns "" if the user does not exist.
  • RESTORE_USER <userId>: restore userId's files to what they were in the latest backup. Returns the number of files successfully restored; returns "" if the user does not exist.

RESTORE_USER runs in these three steps:

  1. Delete all files userId currently owns.
  2. For each (name, size) in the backup: if no file with that name exists now, recreate it with the size from the backup, owned by userId, and count it as one successful restore. If the name is now a file owned by someone else (another user or "admin"), skip it and leave the other file untouched.
  3. Return the number of files created in step 2.

Additional rules:

  • If the user has never made a backup, treat it as "the backup is empty": all of its files are deleted, and it returns "0".
  • A restore does not consume the backup. The same backup can be restored many times.
  • A restore does not change the user's capacity limit. After a restore, remaining capacity = capacity limit − total size of the restored files.
  • A file that is owned by userId both at backup time and now is deleted in step 1, recreated in step 2 with the size from the backup, and also counts toward the returned number.
  • MERGE_USER does not change userId1's backup: that backup still contains only the files userId1 itself owned when it made the backup. userId2's backup is deleted along with userId2.
["ADD_USER", "user", "100"]                        -> "true"
["ADD_FILE_BY", "user", "/dir/file1", "50"]        -> "50"
["ADD_FILE_BY", "user", "/file2.txt", "30"]        -> "20"
["RESTORE_USER", "user"]                           -> "0"      # no backup: both files are deleted
["ADD_FILE_BY", "user", "/file3.mp4", "60"]        -> "40"
["ADD_FILE_BY", "user", "/file4.txt", "10"]        -> "30"
["BACKUP_USER", "user"]                            -> "2"
["DELETE_FILE", "/file3.mp4"]                      -> "60"
["DELETE_FILE", "/file4.txt"]                      -> "10"
["ADD_FILE", "/file3.mp4", "140"]                  -> "true"   # admin takes this name
["ADD_FILE_BY", "user", "/dir/file5.new", "20"]    -> "80"
["RESTORE_USER", "user"]                           -> "1"      # file5.new deleted; file4.txt restored; file3.mp4 skipped
solution:
Settle two things first, and all four levels get easier:

  • Strings are handled only at the outermost layer. The class inside uses normal Python types: numbers are int, failure is False or None. solution converts arguments to numbers and then converts the results to the strings the problem asks for. That way every method is easy to write and easy to test, and the output format appears in only one place.
  • Adding and removing a file each have exactly one entry point (_create, _remove). When Level 3 adds "who owns it" to files, only these two functions need to change, instead of patching bookkeeping code everywhere.

Below, each level adds its features in a subclass, which makes it easy to show the solution in stages. In the real assessment you would simply change the same class.

Level 1

One dictionary, name → size. Each of the three operations is a single hash lookup, O(1) on average (plus the time to hash the name).

class StorageL1:
    def __init__(self):
        self.size = {}                       # file name -> size

    def add_file(self, name, size):
        if name in self.size:
            return False
        self._create(name, size)
        return True

    def get_file_size(self, name):
        return self.size.get(name)           # None if there is no such file

    def delete_file(self, name):
        if name not in self.size:
            return None
        return self._remove(name)

    # The only two places that add or remove a file. Later levels extend them.
    def _create(self, name, size):
        self.size[name] = size

    def _remove(self, name):
        return self.size.pop(name)

Level 2

Scan all files once, keep those whose names start with prefix, sort, and take the first n. The sort key is (-size, name): negating the size turns "size descending, name ascending" into a single ordinary ascending sort.

With F files in total and M matching: filtering takes F prefix comparisons, and sorting takes O(MlogM) comparisons. At the scale of 104 commands that is plenty.

class StorageL2(StorageL1):
    def get_n_largest(self, prefix, n):
        matches = [(name, size) for name, size in self.size.items() if name.startswith(prefix)]
        matches.sort(key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))       # size descending, then name ascending
        return matches[:n]

Level 3

Each file additionally records an owner; each user records three things: the capacity limit limit, the bytes used used, and the set of file names it owns names. "admin" is not put into these three tables: it has no limit and needs no bookkeeping, so the checks simply route around it.

The invariant to maintain: for each user, used equals the total size of the files in names, and used <= limit. Every addition and removal goes through _create and _remove, and used and names are updated in those two places, so the invariant can't be missed. DELETE_FILE calls the same _remove, so "deleting a file gives the space back to its owner" needs no separate code.

MERGE_USER: the files change owner, used adds up, and limit adds up. The statement's "remaining capacities also add up" and "limits add up" are the same thing: remaining = limit − used; both terms add up, so the difference adds up too. In the example, 10+60=70.

Complexity: ADD_USER and ADD_FILE_BY are O(1) on average; MERGE_USER is O(k), where k is the number of files userId2 owns.

ADMIN = "admin"


class StorageL3(StorageL2):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.owner = {}                      # file name -> user id, or ADMIN
        self.limit = {}                      # user id -> capacity limit    (ADMIN is never a key of these three)
        self.used = {}                       # user id -> total size of the files it owns
        self.names = {}                      # user id -> set of the file names it owns

    def _create(self, name, size, owner=ADMIN):
        super()._create(name, size)
        self.owner[name] = owner
        if owner != ADMIN:
            self.names[owner].add(name)
            self.used[owner] += size

    def _remove(self, name):
        owner = self.owner.pop(name)
        size = super()._remove(name)
        if owner != ADMIN:                   # deleting a file gives its bytes back to the owner
            self.names[owner].remove(name)
            self.used[owner] -= size
        return size

    def remaining(self, user):
        return self.limit[user] - self.used[user]

    def add_user(self, user, capacity):
        if user in self.limit:
            return False
        self.limit[user], self.used[user], self.names[user] = capacity, 0, set()
        return True

    def add_file_by(self, user, name, size):
        if user not in self.limit or name in self.size or size > self.remaining(user):
            return None
        self._create(name, size, user)
        return self.remaining(user)

    def merge_user(self, target, source):
        if target == source or target not in self.limit or source not in self.limit:
            return None
        moved = self.names.pop(source)
        for name in moved:
            self.owner[name] = target
        self.names[target] |= moved
        self.used[target] += self.used.pop(source)
        self.limit[target] += self.limit.pop(source)             # limits add up, so remaining capacities add up
        return self.remaining(target)

Level 4

A backup is a dictionary: name → size. It must be a copy of the state at that moment. If you only store a reference to names[user], later additions and removals change the "backup" along with it.

The restore follows the statement's three steps: first delete all of the user's current files, then check the names in the backup one by one and recreate the ones that aren't taken. Two points are worth thinking through here:

  • How do you tell that "the name is taken by someone else"? After step 1, the user no longer owns any file. So in step 2, if a name is still in the size table, it must belong to someone else, and there is no need to compare owners.
  • Can a restore exceed the capacity? No, so the code does no capacity check, just leaves an assertion. The reasoning: at the moment of the backup, the total size of the files in it did not exceed the limit at that time; the limit can only grow (through merges), never shrink; what is restored is a subset of the backup, and the user's existing files have all been deleted. So after the restore, the space used does not exceed the current limit.

On a merge, delete userId2's backup as well. If you skip this step, a user later created under the same name will "inherit" a backup that doesn't belong to it.

Complexity: BACKUP_USER is O(k), where k is the user's current number of files; RESTORE_USER is O(k+b), where b is the number of files in the backup.

class StorageL4(StorageL3):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.backup = {}                     # user id -> {file name: size}, the latest backup only

    def backup_user(self, user):
        if user not in self.limit:
            return None
        self.backup[user] = {name: self.size[name] for name in self.names[user]}    # a copy, not a reference
        return len(self.backup[user])

    def restore_user(self, user):
        if user not in self.limit:
            return None
        for name in list(self.names[user]):                      # 1. drop everything the user owns now
            self._remove(name)
        restored = 0
        for name, size in self.backup.get(user, {}).items():     # 2. bring back what is not taken by someone else
            if name not in self.size:
                self._create(name, size, user)
                restored += 1
        assert self.used[user] <= self.limit[user]               # cannot fail: see the argument in the text
        return restored

    def merge_user(self, target, source):
        remaining = super().merge_user(target, source)
        if remaining is not None:
            self.backup.pop(source, None)                        # the account is gone, and its backup with it
        return remaining

Finally, the string layer. Note that as_text must check for bool before handling numbers: in Python True is also an int, and if the order is reversed "true" becomes "True".

def as_text(value):
    """The string protocol of the assessment, applied in one place."""
    if value is None:
        return ""
    if isinstance(value, bool):              # must come before int: True is an int in Python
        return "true" if value else "false"
    if isinstance(value, list):
        return ", ".join(f"{name}({size})" for name, size in value)
    return str(value)


def solution(queries):
    storage = StorageL4()
    handlers = {
        "ADD_FILE": lambda name, size: storage.add_file(name, int(size)),
        "GET_FILE_SIZE": storage.get_file_size,
        "DELETE_FILE": storage.delete_file,
        "GET_N_LARGEST": lambda prefix, n: storage.get_n_largest(prefix, int(n)),
        "ADD_USER": lambda user, capacity: storage.add_user(user, int(capacity)),
        "ADD_FILE_BY": lambda user, name, size: storage.add_file_by(user, name, int(size)),
        "MERGE_USER": storage.merge_user,
        "BACKUP_USER": storage.backup_user,
        "RESTORE_USER": storage.restore_user,
    }
    return [as_text(handlers[op](*args)) for op, *args in queries]

Follow-ups

There are many files and GET_N_LARGEST is called very often. How do you speed it up? Two places can change. One is finding the matching files: put all names in a sorted structure; names sharing a prefix form one contiguous run in lexicographic order, so binary-search for the start of that run, then walk forward until the first name that doesn't start with prefix. That costs O(logF+M) comparisons instead of scanning all F. If you keep the sorted names in a Python list, insertions and deletions have to shift elements, which is O(F); to make everything fast you need a balanced tree, or a trie. The other is taking the first n: heapq.nsmallest(n, matches, key=...) is O(Mlogn), which beats a full sort when n is much smaller than M.

What if the problem were changed to "if even one file can't be restored, the whole restore fails and nothing changes"? The other cloud storage page on this site has exactly that rule. The way to write it is check first, then act: first confirm that every name in the backup is either unused now or owned by the user, and only once all of them pass start deleting and creating. This page's rule is "skip what can't be restored", which needs no up-front check, but the return value becomes "how many were restored". The test cases of the two rules don't carry over to each other, so read the statement carefully to see which one it is.

Why does the backup store only names and sizes, and not the capacity limit? Because the statement says a restore does not change the capacity. The other page on this site has the opposite rule: the backup stores the capacity limit too, and a restore sets the limit back as well. Whichever rule applies, when writing the restore you should ask "can the restore exceed the capacity?" and be able to give the reason. This page's reason is in Level 4: the limit only grows, never shrinks, and what is restored is only a subset of the backup.

After a merge, what happens when userId1 restores its backup? All files taken over from userId2 are deleted. The backup contains only userId1's own files from back then, and step 1 of the restore deletes all the files it owns now. This follows directly from the rules, and it is also one of the easiest cases to get wrong: some people merge userId2's backup into userId1's backup during the merge, and the statement explicitly says not to.

Four levels in 90 minutes: how do you budget the time? A few minutes each for the first two levels, saving the time for the last two. After passing each level, run that level's example; entering Level 3 is where you are most likely to break earlier things, because the meanings of ADD_FILE and DELETE_FILE change, so after the change rerun the examples of Levels 1 and 2. Keep the return-value formats ("true", "", ", ") in one function so nothing is missed when they change.

Checks (runnable)

def check_table(table, run):
    got = run([query for query, _ in table])
    want = [answer for _, answer in table]
    assert got == want, (got, want)


for table in (LEVEL1, LEVEL2, LEVEL3, LEVEL4):

# --- 2. edge cases of the stated rules ---
def run(*queries):
    return solution([q.split() for q in queries])


# Level 1-2: the name is free again after a delete; n larger than the number of matches; plain string prefixes
assert run("ADD_FILE /a 5", "DELETE_FILE /a", "ADD_FILE /a 7", "GET_FILE_SIZE /a") == ["true", "5", "true", "7"]
assert run("ADD_FILE /ab 5", "ADD_FILE /a/b 5", "ADD_FILE /b 9", "GET_N_LARGEST /a 10", "GET_N_LARGEST /a 1",
           "GET_N_LARGEST /ab/ 1") == ["true", "true", "true", "/a/b(5), /ab(5)", "/a/b(5)", ""]
assert run("ADD_FILE A 1", "ADD_FILE a 1", "ADD_FILE B 1", "GET_N_LARGEST A 5", "GET_N_LARGEST a 5") == [
    "true", "true", "true", "A(1)", "a(1)"]                      # case sensitive
assert run("ADD_FILE f10 3", "ADD_FILE f9 3", "ADD_FILE f100 3", "GET_N_LARGEST f 3")[-1] == "f10(3), f100(3), f9(3)"

# Level 3: filling the capacity exactly is allowed; unknown users; deleting gives the bytes back to the owner
assert run("ADD_USER u 10", "ADD_FILE_BY u /a 10", "ADD_FILE_BY u /b 1", "ADD_FILE_BY nobody /b 1",
           "DELETE_FILE /a", "ADD_FILE_BY u /b 4", "GET_FILE_SIZE /b") == ["true", "0", "", "", "10", "6", "4"]
# a name is unique across all owners, admin included
assert run("ADD_FILE /a 1", "ADD_USER u 10", "ADD_FILE_BY u /a 1", "ADD_FILE_BY u /b 1", "ADD_FILE /b 1") == [
    "true", "true", "", "9", "false"]
# merge: failures change nothing; limits add up; the merged id is free again and starts empty
assert run("ADD_USER a 10", "ADD_USER b 20", "MERGE_USER a a", "MERGE_USER a c", "MERGE_USER c a",
           "ADD_FILE_BY a /a 7", "ADD_FILE_BY b /b 5", "MERGE_USER a b", "ADD_FILE_BY b /c 1",
           "ADD_USER b 3", "ADD_FILE_BY b /c 3", "DELETE_FILE /b", "ADD_FILE_BY a /d 23", "ADD_FILE_BY a /e 1") == [
    "true", "true", "", "", "", "3", "15", "18", "", "true", "0", "5", "0", ""]

# Level 4
# backup of an unknown user, of no files; a restore does not use the backup up; a newer backup replaces the older
assert run("BACKUP_USER u", "RESTORE_USER u", "ADD_USER u 10", "BACKUP_USER u", "ADD_FILE_BY u /a 4",
           "RESTORE_USER u", "GET_FILE_SIZE /a", "ADD_FILE_BY u /a 4", "BACKUP_USER u", "DELETE_FILE /a",
           "RESTORE_USER u", "DELETE_FILE /a", "RESTORE_USER u", "GET_FILE_SIZE /a") == [
    "", "", "true", "0", "6", "0", "", "6", "1", "4", "1", "4", "1", "4"]
# a file the user owns both at backup time and now is restored with the backed-up size, and it counts
assert run("ADD_USER u 10", "ADD_FILE_BY u /a 4", "BACKUP_USER u", "DELETE_FILE /a", "ADD_FILE_BY u /a 9",
           "RESTORE_USER u", "GET_FILE_SIZE /a", "ADD_FILE_BY u /b 6") == ["true", "6", "1", "4", "1", "1", "4", "0"]
# names taken by another user or by admin are skipped and left alone
assert run("ADD_USER u 10", "ADD_USER v 10", "ADD_FILE_BY u /a 1", "ADD_FILE_BY u /b 2", "ADD_FILE_BY u /c 3",
           "BACKUP_USER u", "DELETE_FILE /a", "DELETE_FILE /b", "ADD_FILE_BY v /a 7", "ADD_FILE /b 99",
           "RESTORE_USER u", "GET_N_LARGEST / 5", "ADD_FILE_BY u /d 7", "ADD_FILE_BY v /e 3") == [
    "true", "true", "9", "7", "4", "3", "1", "2", "3", "true", "1", "/b(99), /a(7), /c(3)", "0", "0"]
# merge keeps the target's backup as it was and throws the source's backup away
assert run("ADD_USER a 10", "ADD_USER b 10", "ADD_FILE_BY a /a 1", "ADD_FILE_BY b /b 2", "BACKUP_USER a",
           "BACKUP_USER b", "MERGE_USER a b", "RESTORE_USER a", "GET_FILE_SIZE /b", "GET_FILE_SIZE /a",
           "ADD_USER b 5", "RESTORE_USER b", "ADD_FILE_BY a /c 19") == [
    "true", "true", "9", "8", "1", "1", "17", "1", "", "1", "true", "0", "0"]
# after a merge the target can own a name that its own backup also lists: its files go first, then the backup returns
assert run("ADD_USER a 10", "ADD_USER b 10", "ADD_FILE_BY a /f 3", "BACKUP_USER a", "DELETE_FILE /f",
           "ADD_FILE_BY b /f 8", "MERGE_USER a b", "RESTORE_USER a", "GET_FILE_SIZE /f") == [
    "true", "true", "7", "1", "3", "2", "12", "1", "3"]


# --- 3. random sequences against an independent, deliberately naive model ---
class SlowStorage:
    """Flat lists, no bookkeeping: every answer is recomputed by scanning."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.rows = []          # [name, size, owner]
        self.users = []         # [user, limit]
        self.snaps = []         # [user, [(name, size), ...]]

    def row(self, name):
        hits = [r for r in self.rows if r[0] == name]
        return hits[0] if hits else None

    def user(self, user):
        hits = [u for u in self.users if u[0] == user]
        return hits[0] if hits else None

    def left(self, user):
        return self.user(user)[1] - sum(r[1] for r in self.rows if r[2] == user)

    def run(self, query):
        op, args = query[0], query[1:]
        if op == "ADD_FILE":
            if self.row(args[0]):
                return "false"
            self.rows.append([args[0], int(args[1]), "admin"])
            return "true"
        if op == "GET_FILE_SIZE":
            r = self.row(args[0])
            return str(r[1]) if r else ""
        if op == "DELETE_FILE":
            r = self.row(args[0])
            if not r:
                return ""
            self.rows.remove(r)
            return str(r[1])
        if op == "GET_N_LARGEST":
            hits = sorted(r[0] for r in self.rows if r[0][:len(args[0])] == args[0])
            hits.sort(key=lambda name: self.row(name)[1], reverse=True)          # stable: names stay ascending
            return ", ".join("%s(%d)" % (name, self.row(name)[1]) for name in hits[:int(args[1])])
        if op == "ADD_USER":
            if self.user(args[0]):
                return "false"
            self.users.append([args[0], int(args[1])])
            return "true"
        if op == "ADD_FILE_BY":
            user, name, size = args[0], args[1], int(args[2])
            if not self.user(user) or self.row(name) or self.left(user) < size:
                return ""
            self.rows.append([name, size, user])
            return str(self.left(user))
        if op == "MERGE_USER":
            a, b = self.user(args[0]), self.user(args[1])
            if not a or not b or a is b:
                return ""
            for r in self.rows:
                if r[2] == b[0]:
                    r[2] = a[0]
            a[1] += b[1]
            self.users.remove(b)
            self.snaps = [s for s in self.snaps if s[0] != b[0]]
            return str(self.left(a[0]))
        if op == "BACKUP_USER":
            if not self.user(args[0]):
                return ""
            self.snaps = [s for s in self.snaps if s[0] != args[0]]
            self.snaps.append([args[0], [(r[0], r[1]) for r in self.rows if r[2] == args[0]]])
            return str(len(self.snaps[-1][1]))
        if op == "RESTORE_USER":
            if not self.user(args[0]):
                return ""
            self.rows = [r for r in self.rows if r[2] != args[0]]
            count = 0
            for snap_user, files in self.snaps:
                if snap_user == args[0]:
                    for name, size in files:
                        if not self.row(name):
                            self.rows.append([name, size, args[0]])
                            count += 1
            assert self.left(args[0]) >= 0
            return str(count)
        raise AssertionError(op)


NAMES = ["/a", "/a/b", "/a/c", "/ab", "/b", "/b/a", "/b/ab", "/c"]
PREFIXES = ["/", "/a", "/a/", "/b", "/b/a", "/c", "/zz"]
USERS = ["u1", "u2", "u3", "u4"]
WEIGHTED_OPS = (["ADD_FILE"] * 3 + ["GET_FILE_SIZE"] + ["DELETE_FILE"] * 5 + ["GET_N_LARGEST"] * 2 + ["ADD_USER"] * 2
                + ["ADD_FILE_BY"] * 8 + ["MERGE_USER"] + ["BACKUP_USER"] * 2 + ["RESTORE_USER"] * 2)


def random_query(rng):
    op = rng.choice(WEIGHTED_OPS)
    if op == "ADD_FILE":
        return [op, rng.choice(NAMES), str(rng.randint(1, 40))]
    if op in ("GET_FILE_SIZE", "DELETE_FILE"):
        return [op, rng.choice(NAMES)]
    if op == "GET_N_LARGEST":
        return [op, rng.choice(PREFIXES), str(rng.randint(1, 5))]
    if op == "ADD_USER":
        return [op, rng.choice(USERS), str(rng.randint(30, 120))]
    if op == "ADD_FILE_BY":
        return [op, rng.choice(USERS), rng.choice(NAMES), str(rng.randint(1, 40))]
    if op == "MERGE_USER":
        return [op, rng.choice(USERS), rng.choice(USERS)]
    return [op, rng.choice(USERS)]


rng = random.Random(2026)
seen = {}                                                    # (operation, kind of answer) -> how often
skipping_restores = 0
for _ in range(2000):
    queries = [random_query(rng) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 150))]
    slow = SlowStorage()
    want = []
    for query in queries:
        op = query[0]
        saved = [len(s[1]) for s in slow.snaps if s[0] == query[1]] if op == "RESTORE_USER" else []
        answer = slow.run(query)
        want.append(answer)
        kind = "empty" if answer == "" else "false" if answer == "false" else "zero" if answer == "0" else "value"
        seen[op, kind] = seen.get((op, kind), 0) + 1
        if saved and int(answer) < saved[0]:
            skipping_restores += 1                           # a backed-up name was taken by someone else
    got = solution(queries)
    assert got == want, (queries, got, want)

for case in [("ADD_FILE", "value"), ("ADD_FILE", "false"), ("GET_FILE_SIZE", "value"), ("GET_FILE_SIZE", "empty"),
             ("DELETE_FILE", "value"), ("DELETE_FILE", "empty"), ("GET_N_LARGEST", "value"), ("GET_N_LARGEST", "empty"),
             ("ADD_USER", "value"), ("ADD_USER", "false"), ("ADD_FILE_BY", "value"), ("ADD_FILE_BY", "empty"),
             ("ADD_FILE_BY", "zero"), ("MERGE_USER", "value"), ("MERGE_USER", "empty"), ("BACKUP_USER", "value"),
             ("BACKUP_USER", "zero"), ("BACKUP_USER", "empty"), ("RESTORE_USER", "value"), ("RESTORE_USER", "zero"),
             ("RESTORE_USER", "empty")]:
    assert seen.get(case, 0) >= 20, (case, seen.get(case, 0))    # every branch was really exercised
assert skipping_restores >= 50, skipping_restores

# --- 4. the levels are layered: an earlier level's class still passes its own table ---
def run_on(cls):
    def run_table(queries):
        storage, out = cls(), []
        for op, *args in queries:
            method = getattr(storage, op.lower())
            out.append(as_text(method(*[int(a) if a.isdigit() else a for a in args])))
        return out
    return run_table


check_table(LEVEL1, run_on(StorageL1))
check_table(LEVEL2, run_on(StorageL2))
check_table(LEVEL3, run_on(StorageL3))
